Topic: The Brachistochrone Problem: The Race of Curves

Target audience: University students (Physics/Engineering/Mathematics)

Section: section_1 — Introduction: The Fastest Path

Lecture lines:
What path connects two points in minimum time?
Straight lines seem intuitive but aren't fastest.
Gravity makes steep drops gain speed quickly.

Planned animations:
Fade in title: The Fastest Path. Color: #FFFFFF.
Draw a straight line between two points. Color: #00FF00.
Animate a particle sliding along the straight line. Color: #FFFF00.

Section: section_2 — Prerequisite Concept: Conservation of Energy

Lecture lines:
Gravity converts potential energy to kinetic energy.
Steeper drops gain velocity much faster.
Higher velocity 'buys' time for later travel.

Planned animations:
Fade in title: Conservation of Energy. Color: #FFFFFF.
Show kinetic energy KE = 0.5 * m * v^2. Color: #FF00FF.
Show potential energy PE = m * g * h. Color: #00FFFF.

Section: section_3 — The Counter-Intuitive Truth: The Cycloid

Lecture lines:
Is the straight line actually the fastest path?
The Cycloid is the true fastest curve.
The Cycloid balances speed and distance perfectly.

Planned animations:
Fade in title: The Cycloid Curve. Color: #FFFFFF.
Draw the cycloid curve between the points. Color: #FF4500.
Compare the cycloid curve with the straight line. Color: #FF4500 and #00FF00.

Section: section_4 — Mathematical Framework: Calculus of Variations

Lecture lines:
We minimize the total travel time integral.
We seek a function, not a single point.
This defines our optimal path curve.

Planned animations:
Fade in title: Calculus of Variations. Color: #FFFFFF.
Visualize functional J[y] = integral of L(x, y, y') dx. Color: #7FFF00.
Highlight the extremum path y(x). Color: #FFD700.

Section: section_5 — Real-World Application

Lecture lines:
Nature frequently optimizes for path efficiency.
Optimal paths govern light through changing media.
Even athletes instinctively utilize Brachistochrone logic.

Planned animations:
Fade in title: Real-World Applications. Color: #FFFFFF.
Show a pendulum clock mechanism animation. Color: #87CEEB.
Show a slide or roller coaster design. Color: #FF6347.

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject
